Pharmacovigilance
 The word Pharmacovigilance derived from 
 Pharmacon : Drug
 Vigilare : to be alert
 The science and activities relating to the detection, assessment, 
understanding, and prevention of adverse effects or any other 
drug-related problems.
 Adverse drug reaction: a response to a drug which is noxious and 
unintended which occur at dose used for prophylaxis, diagnostic 
or therapy of disease (causality directly associated with medicine).
 Adverse event: Causality not directly associated with medicine.
 Anti-histaminics: Sedation causes accident and injury.
 Alpha-blockers: Fall in BP- Fall and fracture

Drug safety monitoring
 To market a drug, the manufacturer must provide evidence of its efficacy and 
safety to the U.S.FOOD and Drug Administration (FDA)
 In Pre-marketing study, the numbers and type of patient used to demonstrate a 
drug`s efficacy and safety are limited.
 Although pre-marketing surveillance cannot provide knowledge of the safety 
or efficacy of the drug at the time of introduction into the market.
 Post-marketing surveillance of drug therefore play an important role to 
discover an undesirable effect that might present at risk.
 It provide additional information on the benefit and risk of the drugs.

text:
FDA Communications
 MedWatch Safety Alerts and Drug Safety Communications
 Potential Signals of Serious Risks/New Safety Information 
Identified from FAERS
 Published literature and scientific meetings
 Teleconferences with foreign regulatory agencies:
 EMA: European Medicines Agency
 International Post-Market Surveillance (IPMS): Canada, 
Australia, New Zealand, Switzerland, and Singapore (via 
written submissions)

Pragmatic trials
• A   c l u s t e r r a n d o m i s e d   c o n t r o l l e d   t r i a l   i s   a   t y p e 
of randomised controlled trial in which groups of subjects (as 
opposed to individual subjects) are randomised. ... 
• What is parallel study in Clinical trials?
• A parallel study is a type of clinical study where two groups of 
treatments, A and B, are given so that one group receives only A while 
another group receives only B. Other names for this type 
of study include "between patient" and "non-crossover".

What is cluster study?
• A cluster randomised controlled trial is a type of randomised 
controlled trial in which groups of subjects are randomised. 
• What is adaptive clinical trial design?
• An adaptive design is defined as a design that allows modifications to 
the trial and/or statistical procedures of the trial after its initiation 
without undermining its validity and integrity.
•  The purpose is to make clinical trials more flexible, efficient and fast.

What is randomised cross over trials?
• A crossover study, or a crossover trial, is a longitudinal study in which 
subjects receive a sequence of different treatments (or exposures). ... 
In a randomized clinical trial, the subjects are randomly assigned to 
different arms of the study which receive different treatments.
• What is pragmatic study?
• to evaluate the efficacy of an intervention in a well-defined and 
controlled setting, whereas the term pragmatic was used for trials 
designed to test the effectiveness of the intervention in a broad 
routine clinical practice.

Pragmatic Approach
• Does it work?
• For whom does it work?
• How much does it cost?
• Of secondary importance – how or why does it or does not work?

Pragmatic Trials
• In the 1960s Schwarz and Llellouch coined the phrase ‘pragmatic trial’.
• In a pragmatic trial the design mimics as closely as possible ROUTINE 
clinical practice, with the exception that patients are randomly 
allocated to treatment.

Advantages of pragmatic trials
• An advantage of the pragmatic approach is that because placebos are 
not used and EFFECTIVENESS is estimated.
• Because conditions mimic routine clinical practice this makes the 
results more applicable to the ‘average’ patient.

Prevalence of Sore Throat
Antibiotics = 37%; None = 35%; Delayed = 30% 
Proportion of patients better by day 3 (P=0.28)

Antibiotics
• Little et al showed that immediate use of antibiotics 
for a sore throat had NO significant effect on the 
resolution of symptoms
• A placebo trial would demonstrate this BUT this trial 
also showed that those who did not get antibiotics 
were less likely to visit their GP again

Pragmatic information
• GPs prescribing antibiotics for uncomplicated sore throats has very 
little, if any, effect 
• Patients prescribed antibiotics are more likely to re-attend when they 
next have a sore throat compared with giving no antibiotics

Cranberry Juice for urinary tract infection
• Avorn et al randomised elderly women to receive cranberrry juice or a 
placebo.
• Outcomes were microbiological (I.e., bacterial counts in urine 
samples).
• Result – Cranberry juice significantly reduced bacteria in the urine.
• SO WHAT – what we need to know is whether it reduces symptoms.

Cranberry conclusion
• First trial was suggestive in that it showed an effect on a SURROGATE 
outcome measure of urinary tract infection.
• The second trial was more definite – cranberry supplementation 
reduces symptoms of urinary tract infection in young women.

Pragmatic with explanatory features
• Many, if not most, pragmatic trials will also include features of 
explanatory studies.  We might measure blood pressure, cholesterol 
or bone mass, to elucidate mechanisms to explain why or why 
something did not work.  
• A RCT of vitamin D injection measured a PTH levels to check the 
treatment was being absorbed.  
• This information can be collected cheaply from pragmatic trials to 
enhance their scientific value.

Summary
• Explanatory trials follow the tradition of very tight control of sample – 
difficult to generalise from results.
• Pragmatic study much more generalisable interested in 
EFFECTIVENESS not too interested in how things work.
• Economic evaluations are best conducted using pragmatic studies.

What do you do?
For an patient with a painful sore throat, you wonder 
whether corticosteroids will help with pain relief? 
• You do a search and find several studies: 
• some suggest that steroids reduce pain; some do not 
• What do you do? 
• Ask a consultant? Peer? Patient?
• Ask research student to find all studies & select the best?
• How do you know which study to believe?

Purpose of systematic reviews
• Provide up to date summary of all published research 
literature
• Allow large amounts of data to be assimilated 
• Provide an objective collation of results of research
• Provide reliable recommendations

Clarify the differences
• Systematic Review
• Narrative Review
• Meta-analysis

Systematic Review or meta-analysis?
• A Systematic Review is a review of a clearly formulated question that 
uses systematic and explicit methods to identify, select and critically 
appraise relevant research, and to collect and analyse data from the 
studies that are included in the review. 
• Statistical methods (meta-analysis) may or may not be used to 
analyse and summarise the results of the included studies.

Narrative vs systematic review
Narrative
• Many questions
• No search methods
• No inclusion criteria
• No combining studies
• Prone to random and 
systematic error
• Provide conflicting 
summaries
Systematic
• One question
• Explicit search
• Reproducible
• Explicit inclusion criteria
• Combine study results
(meta-analysis)
WHY do we need Systematic Reviews?

Benefits of systematic reviews 
• Up to date resource for clinicians
• Starting point for clinical guidelines
• Policy guidance
• Basis for new primary research
• Important for grant funding bodies
• Management guidance
• Research training tool???

Useful Resources
• The Cochrane Collaboration www.thecochranelibrary.com/
• Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (version 5 
updated March 2011)
• CRD www.crd.york.ac.uk/
• The Centre for Reviews and Dissemination is a department of the University 
of York and is part of the National Institute for Health Research
• EPPI-Centre www.eppi.ioe.ac.uk/
• The Evidence for Policy and Practice Information and Co-ordinating Centre, 
Social Science Research Unit,  Institute of Education, University of London.

Steps of a systematic review 
1. Clear answerable question
2. Reproducible search strategy
3. Assessment of literature quality
4. Summary of the evidence
5. Statistical, sensitivity analyses
6. Interpretation 
7. Conclusions, recommendations
8. Published protocol and review

Types of systematic review
• Different research questions require different study designs 
generate different types of review
• Variations occur in
• Research questions asked
• Primary study designs included
• Methods for synthesis
• Approaches to being systematic
• Types of evidence included

Decide on process of synthesis
Factors to consider
• Consistency of outcome measures
• Sub groups 
• Heterogeneity
• Common sense test

Meta analysis
• Meta-analysis and decision analysis have in common that they 
synthesized knowledge. Each method takes parts of the medical 
literature or clinical experience and, based on this information, 
attempts to create a whole answer to a defined problem.
• Meta-analysis is a qualitative and quantitative approach for 
systematically assessing and combining the results of previous studies 
in order to draw conclusions about the body of research. Studies of a 
topic are first systematically identified, and inclusion and exclusion 
criteria are defined. In traditional meta-analysis, data from the 
eligible studies are abstracted or collected from the investigators of 
the study

Advantages of meta-analysis
• Increasing sample size and power 
To detect benefits and harms of a drug or treatment, 
  Good source for evidence-based clinical decision making, 
Ability to assess subgroups effects and rare events, 
Ability of indirect comparison and simultaneous evaluation of 
treatment  therapies   available for special conditions, and 
saving time, resources and money.
cumulative meta-analysis could be  as a tool to detect safety 
signal earlier.

Disadvantages of meta-analysis 
• Susceptibility of the original studies to bias,  
• publication and dissemination bias, 
• practical difficulties of combining results from different studies (i.e., 
variations in study designs, subject characteristics, drug exposures, 
and outcomes), 
• paradoxical results due to combining different studies, 
• potential biased results from manipulation of study selection and 
analytic strategies, and 
• challenges of including advanced study designs (e.g., case- crossover, 
clustered randomized trials.

Meta-analysis
• Meta-analysis is the statistical procedure for combining data from 
multiple studies. When the treatment effect (or effect size) is 
consistent from one study to the next,meta-analysis can be used to 
identify this common effect.
• Meta-analysis is a quantitative, formal, epidemiological study design 
used to systematically assess the results of previous research to 
derive conclusions about that body of research. Typically, but not 
necessarily, the study is based on randomized, controlled clinical trials.

Difference between systemic review and 
Meta-analysis
• A systematic review answers a defined research question by 
collecting and summarising all empirical evidence that fits pre-
specified eligibility criteria.
•  A meta-analysis is the use of statistical methods to summarise the 
results of these studies.

Why do we do meta-analysis
• Meta-analysis is a statistical technique for combining data from 
multiple studies on a particular topic. ... Compared to other study 
designs (such as randomized controlled trials or cohort studies), 
the meta-analysis comes in at the top of the 'levels of evidence' 
pyramid in evidence-based healthcare.
• Advantages:
• a meta-analysis uses a statistical approach to combine the results 
from multiple studies in an effort to increase power (over individual 
studies), improve estimates of the size of the effect and/or to resolve 
uncertainty when reports disagree.

Pharmacoeconomic research 
• Pharmacoeconomic research considers both costs and utilities of 
outcome include 
• cost-minimization, 
• cost-effectiveness,
• cost-utility, and 
• cost-benefit.

Cost-minimization analysis
• Cost-minimization analysis (or cost-identification analysis) assumes 
that alternative treatment result in the same outcome, and value or 
decision is assigned entirely based on the lowest cost. It is 
appropriate only if treatment outcomes or benefits are equivalent 
among the therapies being evaluated.
• Ex. Evaluation of brand name Vs generic (with same outcome or 
indication)

Cost-benefit analysis
• Cost-benefit analysis remains a less common used technique in 
economic assessments of health care in the US, because it is difficult 
to translate all outcomes into monetary measures.
• EX. Pharmacist managed a clinic for a disease  Vs Cardiac rehabilitation 
program.

Cost-effectiveness analysis
• Cost-effectiveness analysis assumes that cost and the effectiveness 
of interventions vary, and uses natural units as outcome measures. 
Consequently, value is assigned by the cost per unit improvement of a 
health status, such as dollars per years of life saved.
• Cost/ mm Hg decrease of Blood pressure in the treatment

Cost-utility analysis
• Cost-utility analysis, a type of cost-effectiveness analysis, often 
presents the outcome as cost per quality-adjusted life-year. The 
advantage of cost-utility analysis is that the utility assignment can be 
generalized to all health states.
• Ex. Cost/ Quality  adjusted life year gained for aspirins and statins or 
both drugs for prevention of coronary heart disease in man.

Experimental Study Design: Randomized 
Controlled Trial (RCT)

Hierarchy of Study Designs: Which design 
is best for cause and effect?

Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT)
• A prospective study comparing the effect of intervention(s) 
against a control group in humans
• One or more interventions: (prophylactic, diagnostic, devices, procedures, 
therapeutic agents)
• Control group: “Placebo” or “Active Drug”
• Placebo-Controlled or Active Drug-Controlled Trials
• Gold standard for determining cause and effect relationship for 
beneficial drug effects

Fundamentals of an RCT
• Design of the study
• Execution of the study
• Analysis and Reporting of Results

RCT Study Design
• What are the questions that will be answered by the study?
• Primary Question
-What is the efficacy of Fidaxomicin vs. Vancomycin in curing 
 C. Dif infection?
• Secondary Questions:
-For patients who were cured by treatment, how long does the 
cure last for and what is the risk of recurrence of infection?
-Which drug is more tolerable?

RCT Study Design
• What are the characteristics of the study participants?
• Inclusion (Eligibility) Criteria
C. Dif infections defined by more than 3 unformed bowel movements 
in the 24 hrs prior to allocation of a treatment and either toxin A or B 
within 48 hrs
• Exclusion Criteria
Patients who had 2 or more episodes in the past 3 months

RCT Study Design
• What are some issues with inclusion/exclusion criteria?
• Inclusion/exclusion criteria are set to identify subjects who will 
most likely benefit from the treatment under investigation
• Internal vs. External Validity
• External Validity/Generalizability: 
• How can we generalize the results from a RCT to a wide patient population 
who do not exactly fit the profile of patients in the RCT?
• Internal Validity: 
• What is the role of bias (confounding, observer, selection, etc…) in the results 
that are reported?

RCT Study Design
• How do RCTs handle bias?
A) Randomization (Random Assignments of Eligible 
Patients to either the experimental treatment or control)
-Randomization Techniques:
u Simple Randomization
u Block Randomization
u Stratified Randomization

RCT Study Design: Stratified Randomization
• What if I know that a certain characteristic may influence 
the response to treatment?
• e.g. previous C. Dif infection in the past 3 month may 
influence response to Fidaxomicin or Vancomycin and I 
would like to identify this influence!
• Create two strata (one for patients who had no C.Dif 
infection in the past three month and one for patients who 
had on C. Dif infection)
• Randomly assign participants in each strata to either 
Fidaxomicin or Vancomycin

To calculate the attack rate of the cholera outbreak in Haiti between
January and October 2010, you can use the following formula:

and October 2010 is approximately 55.29 cases per 1,000 people at risk.

The odds ratio (OR) is a statistical measure used to assess the strength and direction of the
association between two variables, often in case-control studies or other observational studies. It
quantifies the odds of an event occurring in one group compared to the odds of the same event
occurring in another group. To calculate the odds ratio, you typically use a 2x2 contingency table with
the following components:
Exposed Group (E): This group includes individuals who were exposed to a specific risk factor,
treatment, or condition.
Unexposed Group (U): This group includes individuals who were not exposed to the specific risk factor,
treatment, or condition.
Outcome (D): This represents the presence of the event or outcome of interest.
No Outcome (Non-D): This represents the absence of the event or outcome of interest.
Here is the formula for calculating the odds ratio (OR):
OR = (AD / BC)
Where:
AD (Exposed with Outcome): The number of individuals in the exposed group who experienced t

for calculating the odds ratio (OR):
OR = (AD / BC)
Where:
AD (Exposed with Outcome): The number of individuals in the exposed group who experienced the
outcome (D).
BC (Unexposed with Outcome): The number of individuals in the unexposed group who experienced
the outcome (D).
Here's a step-by-step explanation of how to calculate the odds ratio:
Set up a 2x2 contingency table:
Outcome (D) No Outcome (Non-D) Total
Exposed AD BD A
Unexposed AC BC B
Total D Non-D N
Fill in the values:
AD: The number of individuals in the exposed group who experienced the outcome.
BD: The number of individuals in the exposed group who did not experience the outcome.
AC: The number of individuals in the unexposed group who experienced the outcome.
BC: The number of individuals in the unexposed group who did not experience the outcome.
Calculate the odds of the outcome for the exposed group (Odds(D|E)):
Odds(D|E) = AD / BD
Calculate the odds of the outcome for the unexposed group (Odds(D|U)):
Odds(D|U) = AC /

outcome for the exposed group (Odds(D|E)):
Odds(D|E) = AD / BD
Calculate the odds of the outcome for the unexposed group (Odds(D|U)):
Odds(D|U) = AC / BC
Calculate the odds ratio (OR):
OR = Odds(D|E) / Odds(D|U) = (AD / BD) / (AC / BC)
The resulting OR can be greater than 1, indicating a positive association between exposure and the
outcome, less than 1, indicating a negative association, or equal to 1, indicating no association. The
interpretation of the OR depends on the context of the study and research question.

Course Title: Research Methods and Pharmacoepidemiology

epidemiological measures, experimental design, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and 
pharmacoeconomics. It includes modern topics such as Real-World Evidence, Drug Safety, 
Personalized Medicine, Antimicrobial Resistance, Vaccine Epidemiology, Global Health, and 
Regulatory Science, equipping pharmacy students with the essential knowledge and skills needed 
for research and practice.

• Master the principles and applications of pharmacoepidemiology and 
pharmacoeconomics. 
• Learn how to conduct systematic reviews and meta-analyses. 
• Understand the integration of real-world evidence and big data analytics. 
• Develop skills in drug safety, pharmacovigilance, and personalized medicine. 
• Explore global health issues and regulatory science in pharmacoepidemiology.

Learning Outcomes: 
Upon completion, students will: 
• Have a comprehensive understanding of research methods, pharmacoepidemiology, and 
pharmacoeconomics. 
• Be proficient in conducting systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and cost-effectiveness 
analyses. 
• Develop skills in applying RWE, big data analytics, and personalized medicine to clinical 
practice. 
• Be prepared to contribute to global health efforts, regulatory science, and patient safety.
